issues.legal_issue: The absence of a fixed deadline for government sanction of a draft town-planning scheme does not by itself make the statutory process an unreasonable restriction on affected owners.
material_facts: A published draft scheme restricted owners’ ability to deal with their land while government considered whether to sanction it.
The statute required the municipal council to prepare and publish a draft scheme within a limited period after the initial resolution, but set no fixed deadline for government sanction.
The process included public notice, opportunities for objections and suggestions, and consideration of the scheme’s technical and other implications.
The challenge relied on the possibility of prolonged delay rather than a demonstrated instance of arbitrary protraction or mala fide inaction.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a fixed deadline for government sanction was not facially arbitrary because the statutory process implied expeditious consideration and provided sufficient guidance; courts could still grant relief against arbitrary protraction or mala fide inaction in a particular case.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 and the right to property do not require a rigid statutory time limit where the nature and scale of a developmental scheme make one impractical and the statute supplies sufficient guidance for expeditious action. Sections 8, 9, 12 and 15 of the Town Planning Act provide the scheme-making process and restrictions; the court may intervene if authorities cause arbitrary protraction or act mala fide.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law and owner_dealings_are_restricted_during_scheme_process and draft_preparation_has_a_statutory_time_limit and government_sanction_has_no_fixed_deadline and scheme_requires_complex_review and no_actual_arbitrary_delay_is_shown

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law: An affected person challenges the constitutionality of a law governing town-planning schemes.
predicates.owner_dealings_are_restricted_during_sch: The scheme process restricts an owner’s ability to deal with land while the scheme is pending.
predicates.draft_preparation_has_a_statutory_time_l: The law sets a time limit for the responsible local body to prepare and publish a draft scheme.
predicates.government_sanction_has_no_fixed_deadlin: The law does not set a fixed time within which the government must decide whether to sanction the draft scheme.
predicates.scheme_requires_complex_review: The scheme requires consideration of matters such as public objections, technical advice, inquiries, and the scale and consequences of development.
predicates.no_actual_arbitrary_delay_is_shown: The challenger identifies a possible delay but does not establish that the authorities have actually caused arbitrary protraction or acted in bad faith.

issues.definition: When a planning-law challenge concerns restrictions during a complex scheme process, the draft has a statutory deadline, government sanction does not, and no actual arbitrary delay is shown, the missing sanction deadline is not unconstitutional on its face.

issues.legal_issue: Town-planning schemes may be treated as a distinct class from routine compulsory acquisitions when the classification has a rational relation to planned urban improvement.
material_facts: The law established a staged process for preparing, publishing, considering and sanctioning town-improvement schemes.
The process involved public participation and consultation with planning expertise, and schemes could vary substantially in scale and complexity.
The challenged law provided a time limit for preparing and publishing a draft scheme, while the ordinary acquisition law provided a time limit for a different stage of acquisition.
The schemes were directed to planned improvement and development of towns rather than to routine, isolated acquisition projects.
issues.conclusion: The distinct treatment of town-planning schemes was justified by a rational differentia reasonably related to the objective of improving towns and regulating their development.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification where the differentia is intelligible and has a rational relation to the legislative objective. The staged, participatory and technically complex process under sections 8 to 12 of the Town Planning Act distinguishes town-planning schemes from routine acquisition proposals; that distinction is relevant to the objective of planned urban development.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law and scheme_is_for_planned_town_improvement and scheme_process_is_staged_and_participatory and schemes_require_specialized_review and classification_tracks_the_scheme_objective

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law: An affected person challenges the constitutionality of a law governing town-planning schemes.
predicates.scheme_is_for_planned_town_improvement: The acquisition is undertaken to carry out a scheme for improving and regulating the development of a town.
predicates.scheme_process_is_staged_and_participato: The law provides successive stages for preparing and publishing a scheme and receiving public objections or suggestions.
predicates.schemes_require_specialized_review: The schemes may require technical expertise and review of their differing scale, complexity and consequences.
predicates.classification_tracks_the_scheme_objecti: The distinct legal treatment corresponds to the objective of carrying out planned town improvement rather than an unrelated criterion.

issues.definition: Where a challenged classification concerns schemes for planned town improvement and reflects their staged, participatory and specialized process, the schemes may be treated separately for procedure.

issues.legal_issue: Providing a special acquisition procedure for town-planning schemes does not create unconstitutional arbitrary choice merely because another acquisition law could theoretically be used.
material_facts: The Town Planning Act provided a specific acquisition mechanism for land required to implement its schemes.
The legislation expressly modified the application of the ordinary acquisition law for those acquisitions.
In one appeal, the authorities used the ordinary acquisition law only after the special mechanism had been invalidated and was unavailable.
The argument that authorities could choose between the two procedures rested on that example and on the theoretical possibility of using either law.
issues.conclusion: The court rejected the claim of arbitrary choice: acquisition for a town-planning scheme was to proceed through the special statutory mechanism, and the isolated use of the ordinary law after the special mechanism had been invalidated did not establish a real choice between procedures.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a fanciful possibility of discriminatory choice is insufficient; the real risk of discrimination must be considered in light of normal administrative conduct. Maganlal v. Municipal Corporation was relied on for that approach. Sections 32 and 34 of the Town Planning Act establish a special acquisition and compensation mechanism, with specified modifications to the ordinary acquisition law.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law: An affected person challenges the constitutionality of a law governing town-planning schemes.
predicates.land_is_required_for_a_town_planning_sch: The land is needed to implement a scheme governed by the special planning law.
predicates.the_special_law_provides_an_acquisition_: The planning law provides a specific procedure for acquiring land needed for its schemes.
predicates.ordinary_law_was_used_only_after_the_spe: The authorities used the ordinary acquisition procedure only after the special procedure had been invalidated or otherwise could not be used.

issues.definition: When land is needed for a planning scheme, a special acquisition procedure exists, and the ordinary procedure was used only because the special procedure was unavailable, the theoretical possibility of choosing between procedures is not arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: Excluding the compensation provision that supplies solatium creates unconstitutional unequal compensation, but the exclusion is severable from the rest of the special compensation scheme.
material_facts: Owners whose lands were acquired for town-improvement schemes received compensation under the special law without solatium because a provision of the ordinary acquisition law was excluded.
The ordinary acquisition law provided solatium to owners whose lands were acquired under it.
The difference in compensation rested on the purpose or statutory route of acquisition, not on a relevant difference between the owners or their land.
The rest of the special compensation mechanism could operate without the exclusion.
issues.conclusion: The exclusion of the provision allowing solatium was unconstitutional under Article 14 but severable; the exclusion was removed, leaving the rest of the special scheme in force and entitling owners to the same compensation, including solatium, available under the ordinary acquisition law.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not permit different compensation for otherwise comparable owners merely because land is acquired for different public purposes or under different acquisition laws, absent a rational differentia related to compensation. The court relied on Vajravelu Mudaliar, Durganath Sharma, Nagpur Improvement Trust and Om Prakash. Under Article 13, only the part of a provision that contravenes a fundamental right is void where it can be severed; the court therefore excised the exclusion of section 25 of the Land Acquisition Act from section 34(1) of the Town Planning Act and applied the corresponding solatium provision.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law and land_is_compulsorily_acquired_for_a_planning_scheme and comparable_owners_receive_different_compensation and difference_depends_only_on_public_purpose_or_acquisition_route and no_compensation_related_differentia_justifies_the_difference and offending_exclusion_is_severable

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_planning_law: An affected person challenges the constitutionality of a law governing town-planning schemes.
predicates.land_is_compulsorily_acquired_for_a_plan: The state compulsorily acquires land to implement a town-planning scheme.
predicates.comparable_owners_receive_different_comp: Owners in comparable compulsory acquisitions receive different compensation, including the availability of an additional payment for compulsory taking.
predicates.difference_depends_only_on_public_purpos: The compensation difference follows only from the public purpose or the acquisition procedure used.
predicates.no_compensation_related_differentia_just: No relevant difference between the owners or their lands rationally explains the difference in compensation.
predicates.offending_exclusion_is_severable: The discriminatory exclusion can be removed without invalidating the remainder of the compensation scheme.

issues.definition: When comparable owners in compulsory planning acquisitions receive different compensation solely because of the public purpose or acquisition route, no relevant justification exists, and the exclusion can be severed, the discriminatory exclusion is removed.
